prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose, rooted in a poetic imagination, that builds an encyclopedic personal cosmology from memory, the body and dream.

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged: Cărtărescu is still my first choice, on the test of a voice found in this writer's work and nowhere else. On public knowledge, Blinding (the Orbitor cycle) and Solenoid join memory, the body and dream in one extended metaphysical project, in a rhythmically dense prose that does not read like anyone else's. The achievement is formal as well as imaginative, because the architecture is built across volumes and not inside a single book. Round 1 sharpened the scope of the citation. It should rest on the prose project, with the poetry named only as the imaginative ground it grew from, because my knowledge of the poetry and its translation coverage are both thin. This is the chair's question about whether poetry belongs in the citation. I would keep the phrase 'rooted in a poetic imagination' and make no co-equal claim for the poems. My alternatives have changed in one respect. I replace Michon (B025) with Carson (B012) as a second alternative. Carlberg and Palm answered my main doubt about Carson, whether the learned apparatus is a game or the route to the feeling, by pointing to grief and desire in Nox and Autobiography of Red. I cannot test that answer by close reading here, but it is a serious one and I no longer treat her case as secondary. Tawada (B001) remains my first alternative. I make these judgments from public knowledge and have not independently verified or re-read any text.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved. I cannot say from this evidence whether the encyclopedic, self-reflexive mode deepens across the largest novels or hardens into repetition of motifs. A related risk is that the effect I praise lives in long, rhythmically complex Romanian sentences that translation may flatten, so my confidence in the voice is partly confidence in translators. Sem-Sandberg, Palm and Carlberg raise the same question about depth or excess. My coverage of the poetry and essays is also uneven, so a whole-oeuvre judgment is only partial. A final concern is that cumulative architecture is one standard of sustained achievement and not the only one. Palm argues that a renewal of what poetry and the essay can do is also an achievement of sustained significance, and I cannot show that scale should outrank it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first for a remaking of Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and argument with inherited forms. He says the question is which body of work shows the more securely established achievement in its own language, and he concedes that translation limits what he can show and that the later collections are the real unknown.
responses.response: I take your case seriously, and I think you have framed the decisive question correctly. I do not hold the translation problem against Adonis alone, since it applies to Cărtărescu too. My position is narrower. The architecture of a prose cycle can be checked more directly in translation than the sound and allusion of Arabic poetry, so I can say more about what I would be crediting. I agree with your answer to Sem-Sandberg's point: uncertainty should not decide the matter on its own, because that would favour writers who translate most readily. That is why I do not move Adonis down on translation grounds. I just cannot assess his case firmly enough to put it first. One correction on the record: the point about age and timing appears in your file's account of my position, but my own round-1 text does not argue it, and I agree it is not a literary criterion. If the Academy's Arabic-poetry specialists could show that the later collections sustain the early level, that would change how I weigh your candidate, and I would say so.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and says the test of sustained quality is whether the later volumes, Solenoid especially, deepen the architecture of the earlier cycle or re-run its obsessions. He proposes anchoring the citation in the prose project with the poetry as foundation.
responses.response: I agree on both points, and my revised citation follows that scope. On the chair's request for specifics, without quoting or claiming a close reading I have not done here, the features I would test are structural. Do the recurring figures of the body, memory and the city change their function between the earlier cycle and Solenoid, or are they only re-presented? Does the late work add a new formal problem, or only more scale? Neither of us can settle that from a summary, and I would not let the strength of our shared preference stand in for it. I also hold to my earlier reply that wider translation is not evidence of quality. It makes the work easier to read, but it does not tell us whether the intensity holds across the largest volumes.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and answers my 'learned game' question by pointing to the emotional register of Nox and Autobiography of Red, where the apparatus serves grief or longing. She says she defers to me on breadth, and that the will does not require a large-architecture standard.
responses.response: That answer moves me more than I expected, and it is the reason Carson is now my second alternative. If the scholarship is the route to the feeling and not a display above it, my chief objection to her falls. Two things remain. First, her most radical books depend on design and typography that I cannot judge from the text. Second, I cannot show that her later work matches the best-known books. I accept your point that large-scale architecture is not the only standard the will supports, and I will not treat it as the only measure of sustained significance. My difference with you is a judgment about which oeuvre is more decisive on voice and depth. I do not think scale and formal renewal can be ranked by a rule, so I am not claiming more than a close, honest preference.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She says the citation for Carson should name the encounter between ancient and modern writing and the formal invention it produces, rest on the core books and not on hybridity alone, and treat translations as context. She treats Cărtărescu as a strong alternative but not an equal on her evidence.
responses.response: Your restriction of the citation to the core books and the formal intelligence is the right discipline. It answers Sem-Sandberg's doubt about the weaker peripheral projects as well as my own. I agree that unevenness among occasional pieces should not count against a core of sustained work. We seem to share the view that the translation uncertainty applies to both candidates and does not separate them. That bears on the chair's question about using shared uncertainty to separate candidates it does not actually separate. Where we differ is the order. I still weigh Cărtărescu's cumulative project slightly higher, but I could support Carson as laureate on the criteria, and I would want her citation to name the original writing and not the scholarship.

responses.point: Sward ranks Tawada first and argues that the bilingual practice is the formal achievement and that the citation should name both Japanese and German. She weighs formal variety across genres above scale and says the same translation uncertainty applies to Cărtărescu and Tawada.
responses.response: I agree that the translation uncertainty does not separate us, and I agree that the citation should name both languages. I would add, as the chair asks, which of the other leading candidates I could support if mine does not reach a majority. On the stated criteria, Tawada is my first alternative because the distributed formal method across genres is a real achievement, and the point that it does not depend on one book answers the single-work worry. The open question for me is the one you name yourself: whether the later novels carry the same formal invention as the earlier work, and whether we are judging a partial corpus when poetry and drama are least visible. I would want that tested against texts read in both languages. If it holds, I would not call the difference between us one of quality.

uncertainties: Whether the encyclopedic, self-reflexive mode of the largest Cărtărescu novels deepens or repeats cannot be settled from the supplied evidence; it needs close reading by readers of Romanian.
How far the rhythmically dense Romanian prose survives translation, and whether the translated editions are a reliable guide to the original.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and essays in translation is thin, so the whole-oeuvre judgment is partial and the citation names poetry only as ground.
Whether cumulative architecture or formal renewal across genres is the better measure of sustained significance under the will's framing is a contested judgment that I have not resolved.
How to weigh Carson's design-dependent works, and whether her later work matches Nox and Autobiography of Red.
How to weigh Tawada's two-language corpus, including the poetry and drama that are least visible in translation, and whether the later novels match the earlier ones.
Adonis's prosodic achievement and the later collections cannot be assessed in the original; this is a limit on my judgment and not a mark against him.
All my judgments rest on public knowledge and the supplied summaries; I have not independently verified or re-read any work, and I cannot measure translation coverage.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It records no personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer. My own practice in historical and psychological fiction is context only and is not treated as evidence of a preference for any candidate. This note updates nothing from round 1.
